analogy.p: Imagine DNA is a recipe book and each gene is a recipe written in three-letter words. Every time the book is copied, a typing mistake can slip in. Most typos are in the margins (non-coding DNA) or change a word to a synonym (same amino acid), so the cake tastes the same. Occasionally a typo changes 'add sugar' to 'add salt' (a different amino acid), and the cake comes out differently. Very rarely the new recipe turns out better, which is a beneficial mutation. Environmental variation is like using a different oven: the same recipe gives different cakes depending on the temperature. The analogy breaks down because real mutations are random chemical changes, not human errors, and the organism does not 'taste' the result; natural selection does.
analogy.t: Mutation as a typing error in a recipe

bullets: **Variation** is needed for evolution by natural selection: if all individuals were identical there would be nothing for the environment to select.
**Within a species** there is variation between individuals; **between species** there are bigger differences.
Variation is found in **animals, plants and microorganisms**, including bacteria.

Some characteristics have **only a few distinct categories** (for example blood group A, B, AB or O), while others show a **range of values** (height, mass). Data on these is plotted in different ways: bar charts for categories, histograms or line graphs for ranges.
Offspring of sexual reproduction are never identical to their parents or to each other (except identical twins), because of how genes are shuffled.
Link to other topics: this is the first step of the story of evolution: variation, then selection, then survival and reproduction, then inheritance.
core.p: **Variation** is the **differences in the characteristics of individuals in a population**. No two living things are exactly alike, even within the same species, and even brothers and sisters differ from each other. A **population** is all the organisms of one species living in a particular area. Variation can be seen in every kind of characteristic: height, hair colour, leaf size, flower colour, blood group, running speed, and so on. AQA expects you to explain that variation arises from **genes (genetic causes)**, from **the conditions in which organisms have developed (environmental causes)**, or from **a combination of both**.

bullets: **Meiosis shuffles alleles:** during the formation of gametes, chromosomes are separated randomly, so each gamete receives a different mixture of the parents' alleles.
**Random fertilisation:** any sperm can fuse with any egg, so the combination of alleles in the zygote is random.
**Two parents:** offspring inherit a mixture of genes from both parents, so they are different from each parent and from siblings.
**Mutation** produces brand new alleles, which is the original source of all genetic variation.
Examples of mostly genetic characteristics in humans: **eye colour, blood group, inherited disorders** such as cystic fibrosis, and natural hair colour.
**Asexual reproduction** produces genetically identical clones, so any differences between the offspring are due to the environment (or a rare mutation).
Link to other topics: sexual and asexual reproduction, meiosis, genetic inheritance.
core.p: **Genetic variation** is caused by differences in the **alleles** that individuals inherit from their parents. Inside a species everyone has the same genes in the same places, but different versions (alleles) of many of them. In **sexual reproduction** these alleles are mixed in several ways, so each gamete and each offspring is unique. A characteristic that is controlled only by genes cannot be changed by the environment, for example **blood group** or **eye colour** (inherited genes).

bullets: **Plants:** a plant in a sunny spot grows differently from a genetically identical plant in the shade; mineral deficiencies cause stunted growth and yellow leaves; leaf size depends on water supply.
**Animals:** the same species can differ in body mass or size because of the **amount and type of food** available.
**Humans:** scars, tattoos, a suntan, a person's accent and language, and a muscle build from exercise are all environmental or acquired characteristics.
**Accidents** (such as losing a finger) and **diseases** that change appearance are environmental influences.
Environmental variation is **not passed on** in the genes to offspring, because the DNA in the gametes has not been changed. A body builder's children will not be born with large muscles.
Studies of **identical twins** raised apart show how environment alone causes differences, because the genes of identical twins are the same.
Link to other topics: plant adaptations, nutrition and the effect of limiting factors on growth.
core.p: **Environmental variation** is caused by the **conditions in which an organism develops and lives**. The environment includes climate, food and nutrient supply, light, water, temperature, accidents, disease and lifestyle. Even organisms with identical genes can look different when the environment differs. Environmental causes can produce differences in any organism, though in some cases the effect is small.

bullets: **Height:** inherited genes decide the possible height, while nutrition and health in childhood affect the height actually achieved.
**Body mass:** genes affect metabolism and appetite, while diet and exercise change the mass.
**Skin colour:** the alleles inherited determine the amount of pigment that can be made, and exposure to sunlight (the environment) changes the amount, causing tanning.
**Plant height or leaf colour:** the genes give the potential, while light, water and minerals decide the actual growth.
**Intelligence and sporting ability:** controlled by many genes and by upbringing, training and opportunity.

To find out which effect is stronger, scientists compare **identical twins** (same genes, different environments) and **non-identical or unrelated individuals** (different genes, similar environments).
Link to other topics: the idea of a **phenotype** being the result of genotype plus environment.
core.h: Variation caused by both genes and environment
core.p: Many characteristics are controlled by **both** the genes you inherit and the environment in which you live. The genes set the **potential** for a characteristic, and the environment affects how much of that potential is reached. A person may inherit genes for being tall, but if they have a poor diet while growing, they may not reach their full height. This combined influence is very common and is why many exam questions involve identifying which factor causes a particular difference.

bullets: **Independent variable:** the environmental factor you change (for example light intensity).
**Dependent variable:** the characteristic you measure (for example mean height of the plants in cm).
**Control variables:** keep everything else the same (temperature, volume of water, type and mass of soil, species and age of plants).
Use a **large sample** and calculate a **mean** to reduce the effect of random differences between individuals.
**Repeat** the investigation to check the results are reliable and look out for anomalies.

**Conclusion example:** because the plants were clones (identical genes), the difference in height must have been caused by the different light conditions, so light is an environmental cause of variation.
Safety and ethics: handle scissors and soil safely, wash hands after handling plants and soil, and be careful with electrical equipment such as lamps near water.
core.p: You may be asked to **plan or evaluate an investigation** into variation. A good investigation controls variables so that a difference can be assigned to the environment or to genes. A classic approach is to take **genetically identical** organisms (clones, such as cuttings from the same plant, or seeds from a pure-breeding line) and grow them in **different conditions**. Any difference in growth must be due to the environment. In contrast, grow **genetically different** organisms in the **same** conditions, and any differences are likely to be genetic.

bullets: **Discontinuous:** blood group, tongue rolling, flower colour in pea plants; usually controlled by one or two genes with little effect from the environment.
**Continuous:** height, mass, leaf length; usually controlled by many genes and affected by the environment.
Discontinuous data are shown in a **bar chart** with gaps between the bars.
Continuous data are shown in a **histogram** (bars touching) or a **frequency polygon**; most individuals are near the mean and few are at the extremes.
When describing a graph, give the **range**, the **most common value (mode)**, and the **overall shape**, using numbers from the axes.
Link to other topics: sampling and statistics in the working scientifically skills (mean, mode, median, range).
core.p: Variation in a characteristic can take two forms, which helps you decide how to display data. In **discontinuous variation** the characteristic can only be in a few distinct categories with no values in between (for example blood group). In **continuous variation** the characteristic can have any value within a range (for example height or mass) and often shows a bell-shaped (normal) distribution. This distinction is useful for data and graph questions, even though AQA focuses on the causes of variation.

bullets: Mutations **occur continuously** in all organisms, usually as rare mistakes when DNA is copied before cell division.
**Substitution:** one base is replaced by a different one; **insertion:** an extra base is added; **deletion:** a base is lost.
Mutations are **random**: they are not directed by the needs of the organism. A mutation does not happen because it would be useful.
A mutation in a **body cell** can affect only the individual (for example it may lead to cancer); a mutation in a **gamete** can be passed to offspring.
Mutations can be **harmful, neutral or beneficial**, depending on their effect on the phenotype and on the environment.
A mutation that makes a new allele can give rise to a **new characteristic** (phenotype) that did not exist before.
Link to other topics: DNA structure, protein synthesis, inherited disorders, cancer.
core.p: A **mutation** is a **random change in the base sequence of DNA**. It can be a change of one base for another (substitution), the loss of a base (deletion), or the addition of a base (insertion). Because the sequence of bases in a gene determines the order of amino acids in a protein, a mutation may alter the protein. Mutations are the **source of new alleles**: every allele in a population started as a mutation in the past.

bullets: **Ionising radiation** includes X-rays, gamma rays and UV light. It can break DNA or change bases.
**Chemical mutagens** include some chemicals in cigarette smoke (such as tar) and certain industrial chemicals.
**Protective measures:** wear sun cream and avoid sunbeds to reduce UV exposure, use lead shielding and limit the number of X-rays, and avoid smoking.
Radiation workers wear dosimeter badges and protective clothing to limit exposure.
Mutations are **more likely** with greater exposure, so people with higher exposure (for example heavy smokers) have a higher risk of mutations leading to cancer.
Because most DNA damage is repaired, a mutagen increases the **chance** of a mutation; it does not guarantee one.
Link to other topics: ionising radiation in the Physics section, cancer in the cell division topic, and non-communicable diseases.
core.p: Mutations occur **spontaneously and continuously** because of random errors in copying DNA. However, the **rate** of mutation is **increased** by exposure to certain things. **Ionising radiation** (such as X-rays, gamma rays and ultraviolet light) can damage DNA directly, and some **chemicals** (such as those in tobacco smoke) also cause DNA damage. Substances and radiation that cause mutations are called **mutagens**. Because mutations in body cells can lead to uncontrolled cell division, some mutagens are also **carcinogens**, which cause cancer.

bullets: Much of the DNA is **non-coding** (it does not code for a protein), so a change in these regions often has no effect on the protein made.
Even in a gene, a change may mean the **same amino acid** is still coded for (Higher: several different triplets can code for the same amino acid), so the protein is unchanged.
If the amino acid changes, the protein may still **fold into nearly the same shape** and work almost normally.
A mutation may occur in a part of a protein that is **not important for function**.
Mutations in **gametes** are rarely noticed unless they affect the phenotype of the offspring.
A mutation **in body cells** is usually repaired or only affects a few cells, so the individual is not noticeably affected.
Very rarely a mutation changes the protein enough to give a **new phenotype**, which is the reason the phrase 'very rarely' appears in the specification.
core.h: Most mutations have little or no effect
core.p: AQA states that **most mutations do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly**, so the phenotype does not change. Only **very rarely** does a mutation lead to a new phenotype. There are several reasons why most mutations have little effect, and giving these reasons earns marks in explain questions.

bullets: Step 1: a base in the DNA sequence of a gene is changed (substitution, insertion or deletion).
Step 2: the new base sequence means a different triplet, so a **different amino acid** may be added in protein synthesis.
Step 3: the **sequence of amino acids** is different, so the chain folds differently.
Step 4: the protein has a **different shape**, so it may not carry out its function (for example, an enzyme no longer binds its substrate).
Step 5: the change in function may lead to a **different characteristic (phenotype)** such as a disorder.
**Insertions and deletions** can have a bigger effect than substitutions because they can **shift the triplets** after the mutation (a frameshift), changing many amino acids.
**Non-coding DNA:** these parts of DNA can **switch genes on and off**, so a mutation in them may change how much of a protein is made (gene expression) without changing the protein itself.
Link to other topics: protein synthesis, enzyme structure and active site, the lock and key model.
core.h: Higher tier: how a mutation changes a protein
core.p: A gene is a sequence of bases in **triplets (groups of three)**. Each triplet codes for a particular **amino acid**, and the order of amino acids determines how the protein **folds** to form its shape. If a mutation changes a base, it may change the triplet and therefore the amino acid. This can alter how the polypeptide folds, so the protein has a **different shape** and may no longer work. For an **enzyme**, a change in shape of the **active site** means the substrate no longer fits; for a **structural protein**, it may be weaker.

bullets: **Mutation** makes a new allele, which may cause a new phenotype.
If the phenotype gives an **advantage**, those organisms are more likely to **survive and reproduce**.
They pass on the advantageous allele to offspring, so over many generations the allele becomes more common.

**Example: antibiotic resistance in bacteria.** A random mutation makes a bacterium resistant. When antibiotics are used, non-resistant bacteria die and resistant bacteria survive, reproduce quickly and the whole population becomes resistant. (MRSA is a well-known resistant strain.)
**Example: pesticide resistance in insects** follows the same pattern.
The change can be rapid when the species reproduces quickly (such as bacteria) because many generations occur in a short time.
A mutation that is harmful or neutral will not become common unless the environment changes; harmful alleles tend to be removed by natural selection.
Link to other topics: natural selection, resistant bacteria, theories of evolution.
core.p: A mutation that produces a **new allele** gives a new version of a gene. If the new phenotype is **suited to the environment** (or the environment changes so that it becomes an advantage), the organisms with it are more likely to survive and reproduce. They pass on the new allele, so it becomes more common in the population over generations. If this happens a lot, it can lead to **relatively rapid change in the species**. This is why mutations are essential for evolution by natural selection.

bullets: **Harmful:** the mutation that creates the **cystic fibrosis allele** results in a faulty membrane protein; the person has thick sticky mucus and breathing problems.
**Harmful:** mutations in genes controlling **cell division** can cause **uncontrolled cell division**, forming a tumour that may become cancer.
**Neutral:** many mutations in non-coding DNA or that change a base without altering the amino acid have no effect on the phenotype.
**Beneficial:** a mutation that gives bacteria **resistance to an antibiotic** is beneficial to the bacteria when the antibiotic is present.
**Beneficial (depending on environment):** a mutation producing darker colouring in an animal may help it hide in a dark habitat.
Whether a mutation is called beneficial or harmful depends on whether it increases or decreases the organism's **chance of survival and reproduction**.
Link to other topics: inherited disorders, cancer, natural selection.
core.h: Harmful, neutral and beneficial mutations: examples
core.p: The effect of a mutation depends on what protein is affected and on the environment. In the same species, the same mutation can be harmful in one environment and useful in another. You should be able to give an example of each type, linked to the idea of phenotypes.

bullets: For **identical twins**, say the genes are the same so differences are environmental.
When comparing two sets of data, quote values and say which is bigger, then **explain the cause** (genetic, environmental or both).
Always link a mutation to **a change in the base sequence**, then to a **different protein**, then to a **new phenotype**, in a clear chain.
Do not say mutations 'happen on purpose' or that organisms 'need' a mutation; they are **random**.
Use a **mean** to compare groups, and mention a **large sample** and **controlled variables** to make the result reliable.
Remember that environmental variation cannot be inherited because it does not change the DNA.
Link to other topics: Working scientifically (planning, graphs, evaluation).
core.h: Exam technique and data skills for variation and mutation
core.p: Questions on this topic mix recall with application. You may have to **describe variation from a graph or table**, **decide whether differences are genetic or environmental**, or **explain why a mutation does or does not change a phenotype**. Use the terms 'allele', 'phenotype', 'protein', 'amino acid' and 'shape' carefully and in the right order.

exam: **1 mark:** 'What is meant by variation?' = differences in characteristics between individuals of a population (1). 'Name one cause of mutations' = ionising radiation / X-rays / chemicals in tobacco smoke (1).
**2 marks, genetic or environmental:** state the cause and justify it, for example 'environmental (1), because identical twins have the same genes (1)'.

**Mutation explanation (3 to 4 marks, Higher):** mutation changes the base sequence (1); different amino acid sequence (1); protein folds into a different shape (1); the protein (for example enzyme) can no longer function (1).
'**Why do most mutations have no effect?**' = much of the DNA is non-coding (1) or the same amino acid is still coded for / the protein shape is unchanged (1).
**Evolution link (4 marks):** new allele arises by a mutation (1); the new phenotype gives an advantage (1); those organisms survive and reproduce (1); allele passed on and becomes more common (1).
**Investigation questions:** identify independent, dependent and control variables, name the equipment (ruler, balance), and state that a large sample and a mean improve reliability.

**Graph and data tips:** quote values with units from the table or axis, compare numbers (for example 'the plant in high light was 30 cm, 18 cm taller than low light') and refer to genes or environment.
**Use the stem:** if the question says 'identical' or 'clones', it is pointing to the genes being the same, so the cause is environmental.
**Command words:** 'Describe' = say what happens; 'Explain' = give a reason with 'because'; 'Suggest' = apply knowledge to an unfamiliar situation.
Include the key words **random**, **continuously** and **very rarely** when writing about mutations, because they match the specification wording.

mistakes.r: Mutations are random; they occur continuously and a new allele is only useful if it happens to suit the environment.
mistakes.w: Mutations happen because the organism needs them.

mistakes.r: Most mutations have no effect or only a slight effect; a few are harmful and very rarely a mutation is beneficial.
Variation can be genetic, environmental, or both.
mistakes.w: Variation is only caused by genes.

mistakes.r: Environmental characteristics do not change the DNA in gametes, so they are not inherited.
mistakes.w: A tan or a scar can be passed on to children.

mistakes.r: A mutation changes the base sequence of DNA, which may change the order of amino acids, so the protein folds into a different shape.
mistakes.w: A mutation changes the protein directly.

mistakes.r: Mutagens increase the rate or chance of mutation; they do not guarantee one.
mistakes.w: Radiation and chemicals make mutations happen every time.

mistakes.r: The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits, which means the enzyme cannot catalyse the reaction.
mistakes.w: A different shape of enzyme means it has changed its function on purpose.

mistakes.r: They have the same genes but different environments, so differences between them are environmental.
mistakes.w: Identical twins are identical in every way.

mistakes.r: Gamete mutations can be inherited, but mutations in body cells can cause cancer; both can matter.

summary: AQA wants you to know that variation is the differences in characteristics between individuals of a population, caused by genes, the environment, or a combination of both, and that mutations are random changes in DNA that occur continuously, are increased by ionising radiation and some chemicals, and only very rarely produce a new phenotype. At Higher tier you must link mutations in coding and non-coding DNA to changes in protein structure and gene expression. It matters because variation and mutation are the raw material for natural selection and evolution.

terms.d: The differences in the characteristics of individuals in a population.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat.
Variation caused by differences in the genes (alleles) inherited.
Variation caused by the conditions in which organisms have developed.
A different version of the same gene.
The characteristics of an organism that are shown, as a result of its genes and environment.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA.
A substance or radiation that increases the rate of mutation.
High-energy radiation, such as X-rays, gamma rays and ultraviolet light, that can damage DNA and cause mutations.
Parts of DNA that do not code for proteins but can switch genes on and off.
A group of three bases in DNA that codes for one amino acid.
A small molecule that is the building block of proteins; the order of amino acids decides the protein's shape.
A molecule made of a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific shape.
Whether a gene is switched on and used to make a protein.
The process by which organisms better adapted to their environment survive and reproduce more, passing on their alleles.
The ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic, which can result from a mutation.
A genetically identical copy of an organism.
A characteristic that can take any value within a range, such as height.
A characteristic that falls into distinct categories with no intermediate values, such as blood group.

worked.ans: Identical twins have exactly the same genes, so the difference in height cannot be caused by different alleles. It must be caused by the environment, for example differences in diet or illness during childhood, which affected how much of their genetic potential for height they reached.
worked.q: Two identical twins were separated at birth. One lives in a city and the other in the countryside. Their heights differ by 4 cm. Explain what caused the difference. (3 marks)
steps: Identical twins have the same genes, so the genes are not the cause.
The difference must be environmental: differences in diet, health or lifestyle during growth.
Link: genes set the potential, environment decides how much is reached.

worked.ans: The mutation changes the base sequence in the gene, so a different triplet codes for a different amino acid. The sequence of amino acids is altered, so the polypeptide folds into a different shape. If the protein is an enzyme, the active site no longer matches the shape of the substrate, so the substrate cannot bind and the enzyme cannot catalyse the reaction.
worked.q: Explain how a mutation in a gene could lead to a protein that no longer works. (4 marks, Higher)
steps: A mutation changes the sequence of bases in the DNA of the gene.
The triplet code changes so a different amino acid is added.
The chain of amino acids folds into a different shape.
If it is an enzyme, the active site is a different shape.

worked.ans: The results show that light intensity affects growth, because the plants are genetically identical so the differences must be environmental (more light gives greater height). The mean height increases by (30 - 12) / 12 x 100 = 150%.
worked.q: A student grew 30 cuttings from one plant. Ten were grown in low light, ten in medium light and ten in high light. After 4 weeks, the mean heights were 12 cm, 21 cm and 30 cm. Explain what the results show and calculate the percentage increase in mean height from low to high light. (4 marks)
steps: Cuttings are clones with the same genes, so differences are environmental.
